It is the twenty-eighth of May, 1453. The sun has gone down behind the walls of Constantinople. For a thousand years, this city has been the heart of an empire. Its domes have outlived emperors, invasions, and plague. But tonight, the lamps are being lit for the last time. Outside the walls, an army waits in the dark. Inside, nine thousand people wait with it. No one speaks loudly. There is nothing left to decide, and nothing left to prepare. Only a few hours remain, and in those hours, ordinary people will do what people have always done on the last night of a world. They will pray. They will hold their children. They will mend a torn cloak, or finish a letter they know may never be sent. My name is the Keeper, and this is the shelf where the old logs are kept. So find a comfortable place. Let your shoulders soften. Let your breathing slow. Let the day fall away from you, the way it always does in the end. Tonight, we open the log of the last night of Constantinople. Let us begin. Before we go inside the city, let us stand outside it for a moment, and look at it the way a traveller would have looked at it, arriving by sea, in the last light of an evening in May. Imagine you are on the deck of a small ship. The wind has dropped. The sail hangs loose. The oars have been taken in.

And ahead of you, low on the water, is a shape you have heard about your whole life. It is not one building. It is a line of hills, crowded with houses, and on those hills, above those houses, there are domes. Many domes. Small ones, and then larger ones, and then one great dome in the middle, so wide that the eye does not believe it at first. That dome belongs to the Church of the Holy Wisdom. Hagia Sophia. In this year, fourteen fifty-three, it is almost a thousand years old. For a thousand years, people have said that when you see it, you understand what an empire is. Now, from the water, the city still looks whole. That is the strange thing about this evening. From a distance, nothing is finished yet. The towers still rise. The lamps still glow in the windows. A bell is still ringing somewhere in the hills, slow and steady, calling people to the evening service. You can hear it over the water, if you listen. One bell. Then silence. Then another. That is the sound of a city doing what it has always done. And that, more than anything else, is what makes this night so quiet. The city is not behaving like a city about to end. It is behaving like a city going to sleep. Let us come closer. The ship passes the sea walls, and here you begin to see the truth of the place. The walls are old. Very old.

Some stones have been reset so many times that they no longer line up with the ones beside them. There are gaps that were filled with rubble, and gaps that were filled with whatever was at hand, and a few gaps that were never filled at all. In places, ivy has taken the wall the way ivy always takes old things. Slowly. Politely. One small green hand at a time. Above the walls, on the highest ground, you can see the shape of the city's spine. The long street that runs from the eastern gate to the western one, the great squares, and the columns that were raised when this city was not called Constantinople at all, but something older. The city has had many names. It has been Byzantium. It has been New Rome. It has been Constantinople. In another hundred years, it will be something else again. But tonight, it is simply the city. To the people inside, it is just home. The place where they were born, where their parents were married, where their children learned to swim, where the bread is bought in the morning and the lamps are lit at night. When we say, the fall of a city, we usually imagine a single moment. A wall breaking. A gate opening. A flag coming down. But a city is not a wall. A city is a thousand small habits. And the last night of a city is not a battle.

It is a thousand small habits, being performed for the last time, by people who know it, and who are trying very hard not to think about it. Let us walk in through a gate that is still open. There is a guard at the gate. He is not young. His cloak is good wool, but it has been mended at the shoulder, and the mending is not recent. He has a spear, and he holds it the way a man holds a tool he has carried for many years. Without thinking about it, and without much affection. He looks at you. He does not challenge you. Tonight, nobody challenges anybody. He simply steps aside, and nods, and lets you pass. Behind him, inside the gate, the street is quiet. There is a smell of woodsmoke and old stone and something baking. There is a woman carrying a clay jar on her hip. There is a boy chasing a chicken, and losing. There is a dog asleep in the exact centre of the street, in the exact place where everyone must walk around him. Nothing about this is dramatic. That is the point. This is what a city looks like on the last night of its life. Not a stage. Not a painting. Just a street, where a dog is asleep, and someone is baking bread, and someone is late for the evening service, and the light is going gold, and then going grey. Let us go up, now, to a place where we can see the whole of it.

The roofs, the water, the walls, and the camp beyond them. There is a tower on the northern side with a window that faces the sea. Someone has left the shutter open. It is a small thing. But it lets the last of the evening in, and it lets the city out. From up here, you can see the lamps being lit. One by one. Then in groups. Then in lines along the streets, until the whole dark shape below you is freckled with warm points of light, like a second sky that has fallen to the ground. Count them, if you like. You will not finish.
